pass.scope: layout + brand half of app-taste (phases 1, 2, 6). Interaction (3), identity (4), moderation (5), re-shoot (7) and submit (8) are NOT part of this pass.

dualThemeContrast.method: computed in-app by palette.ts contrastRatio(), asserted for every pair in TEXT_PAIRS in BOTH themes
dualThemeContrast.worstPairDark: heroSubFg on heroFrom — 4.86:1 (next: brand on surface 5.88:1)
dualThemeContrast.worstPairLight: brand on page — 4.645:1 (next: heroSubFg on heroFrom 4.65:1, then brandFg on brand / brand on surface 4.90:1)
dualThemeContrast.correction: THIS LEDGER NAMED THE WRONG WORST PAIR IN BOTH THEMES AND HAS BEEN RE-MEASURED. It recorded dark worst = brand on surface 5.88 and light worst = brandFg on brand / brand on surface 4.90. Both are real ratios and neither is the minimum: re-derived over all 20 TEXT_PAIRS x both themes with palette.ts's own contrastRatio(), the dark minimum is heroSubFg on heroFrom at 4.859 and the light minimum is brand on page at 4.645. The figures quoted before were the 2nd/3rd-worst rows. Nothing about the palette changes and the AA claim still holds — the global minimum across both themes is 4.645 against a bar of 4.5 — but the MARGIN is thinner than this block advertised: 0.145 rather than the 0.40 that 4.90 implied. App.tsx's heroSubStyle docblock (4.86 dark / 4.65 light) was correct all along and this ledger contradicted it.

sdkVersionAtPass.note: read from the INSTALLED packages in this clone, not from the monorepo. No @civitai/* version was hand-edited by this pass.

heroPrompt: A wide abstract brand banner for a creative video-thumbnail tool. A dark near-black ground with an energetic burst of magenta and cyan light radiating outward from a point on the RIGHT-HAND side of the frame: sharp angular light shards, fine rays and soft volumetric glow, deep perspective, high contrast, cinematic. Rich saturated magenta (hex FF49BD) is the dominant hue with cool electric cyan as the secondary accent. Entirely abstract - pure light, colour and geometry, no objects and no subject. The LEFT half of the frame is almost entirely empty near-black space with only the faintest falloff glow, deliberately left clear. Completely textless.
heroNote: REGENERATED 2026-09-30 on ChatGPT Images v2.0 (--ecosystem OpenAI --checkpoint 2880272), workflow 8753561-20260930160937772-p1wh, quantity 2, dry-run estimate 418 Buzz and realized charge 418 Buzz (equal). Replaces the earlier default-ecosystem render (workflow 8753561-20260930060406237-dxhg, 16 Buzz), whose candidates are still in assets/hero/ alongside this pass's pair in assets/candidates/hero/. TEXTLESS BY DESIGN - unchanged and still the reason: the hero's title stays in the DOM, where it is crisp at any width, follows the theme and is readable by assistive tech. ASPECT - THE PREVIOUS NOTE'S GENERALISATION IS NOW FALSIFIED AND MUST NOT BE RESTATED. It read '--aspect-ratio was REQUESTED and NOT honoured ... the platform ignores requested output size however it is asked', generalising three same-answer routes (SD XL 1.0, FLUX.1 [dev], the default ecosystem, all 1216x832 / 1.46) into a claim about the PLATFORM. OpenAI is a fourth ecosystem and it HONOURS the request exactly, measured at two points in this pass: requested 1:1 came back 1024x1024 (1.000) and requested 16:9 came back 1536x864 (1.778), confirmed both by `magick identify` on the downloaded files and by the workflow's own stored metadata.params.aspectRatio width/height. The honoured/ignored behaviour is therefore ECOSYSTEM-SPECIFIC; measure it per ecosystem rather than assuming either answer. NO MIRROR THIS TIME: the previous render put its burst left of centre and had to be `magick -flop`ped, because heroStyle's scrim is `linear-gradient(90deg, heroTo 0%, heroTo 42%, transparent 82%)` - opaque across the LEFT 42% where the left-aligned DOM title sits, so the image's interest has to live on the RIGHT. This prompt asks for the burst on the right directly and both candidates delivered it, so the committed crop is unflipped. Cropped 1536x480+0+160 (a 3.2 band centred on the burst) then resized to 1216x380 at JPEG quality 88, matching the dimensions heroStyle already paints. PRICING is aspect-dependent on this model in a way a flat per-image figure hides: 1:1 estimated and charged 287/image, 16:9 estimated and charged 209/image. GOTCHA: a '#' in the prompt is consumed server-side as a wildcard/snippet reference - the icon run's stored params show targets.prompt[0].category = 'FF49BD' from a literal '#FF49BD'. This prompt says 'hex FF49BD' instead.

decisions.fork: How does the block decide its shape? Per-call-site breakpoint ternaries, CSS container queries, or one pure function?
decisions.chosen: One pure function, layoutForTier(tier, isUltrawide) in src/layout.ts, returning every decision as a field.
decisions.constraint: A CSS container query CANNOT read a custom property in its prelude — `@container (min-width: var(--civitai-bp-sm))` is silently dead, no error and no warning — so the breakpoints would have to be duplicated as literals in a second place. And this app's only test environment is jsdom, which lays nothing out and evaluates no container queries: a container-query layout could only be asserted as the TEXT of a CSS rule, which type-checks past a wrong value. A function returning numbers can be asserted with literal numbers.

decisions.fork: The content-column cap: keep 640, raise it, or drop it?
decisions.chosen: Cap by COLUMN COUNT, not by tier: 640 at one column (base/xs), 1184 at two (sm/md), uncapped at three or more (lg/xl/ultrawide).
decisions.constraint: A full-page block's column is as wide as the viewport (the host imposes no width — see the ultrawide fork for the measurement) and `maxWidth: 640` was applied on every screen, so most of the block was empty; at 1600px, 60% of it. Dropping the cap everywhere would be the opposite bug — a single text column the full width of the block. Tying it to the column count makes it one rule with one reason. 🔴 THE TWO-COLUMN CAP WAS 1100 AND THAT CONTRADICTED THE ASK. The requirement for this pass was that the layout fill the width on a tablet, and tier `md` runs 1024-1183: a block 1101-1183px wide got a 1100px column centred inside gutters — 40px either side at 1180px, which is the landscape CSS width of the 10.9-inch tablet class, i.e. exactly the device the requirement was about. The original version of this entry recorded only that the cap never binds at `sm`, which is the half that was harmless; it did not record that it DID bind at `md` and broke the ask. Raised to 1184, the `lg` boundary, so the two-column cap cannot bind at any width either tier admits. Consequence stated rather than dressed up: the number now constrains nothing at any reachable width — it is the two-column rung of 'cap by column count' written as a value instead of a special case, and it is not `null` because in layout.ts `null` means 'the rail is on', an invariant layout.test.ts asserts in both directions. Covered by a 1180px arm in responsive.test.tsx and a tier-top invariant in layout.test.ts, both watched RED at 6fcd076 before the change.

decisions.fork: The brief asked for a COLUMN COUNT ladder (1/2/2/3/3/4) on both grids. Apply it to the format picker too?
decisions.chosen: No. The results grid keeps the count ladder; the format picker is sized instead — `auto-fill` with a minimum card width (124 / 160 / 200 / 220 px).
decisions.constraint: A fixed count is wrong for the format grid in BOTH directions. At `base` a one-card-per-row picker gives each of the six built-in formats a ~340px 16:9 preview and makes the picker taller than the phone, where auto-fill at 124px already fits two or three. At `xl` a count of three stretches three cards across ~1000px of main column and makes each preview wider than the thumbnail it previews. What the ask wanted — 'previews at usable size' — is a minimum, so that is what it is.

decisions.fork: Where does ultrawide come from? Extend the tier ladder, or an app-owned threshold?
decisions.chosen: An app-owned boolean hook, useUltrawide(rootRef, threshold = 1800), mirroring useBlockBreakpoint's observe/dedupe/seed discipline.
decisions.constraint: useBlockBreakpoint's top tier `xl` is UNBOUNDED — measured through the real resolveBlockTier, 1440 and 2560 resolve identically — and the hook deliberately exposes no raw width (its own docs: doing so 'would either force a render per pixel or be a lie'). So a fourth column has no tier to hang off. 🔴 1800 RATHER THAN 1440, AND THE REASON FIRST RECORDED HERE WAS STALE. It read '1800 because the live desktop block is ~1600px: a lower threshold would make ultrawide the normal case and leave the 3-column layout unreachable'. That 1600 was the host's own `max-width: 1600px` on the full-page app surface, deleted upstream in civitai 7570507fb8 (2026-09-28, 'App Blocks: uncap the full-page app surface so each app controls its own width') — one day before this pass, so the premise was already gone when it was written. The number survives on different evidence: REACHABILITY OF BOTH BRANCHES, taken from the host. PageBlockHost.tsx gives the content wrapper `width: 100%` and no max-width in any spelling, and the host's own browser suite PageBlockHostMaxWidth.browser.test.tsx asserts the app column equals its parent AND the viewport with zero gutter at 1620 / 1905 / 2560 / 3440. So a maximised 1920x1080 browser hands the block ~1905px, which is over the threshold and makes the 4-column branch something a person actually meets, while 1440-1799 (a windowed browser, a 1600 or 1680 monitor, a scaled laptop panel) stays `xl` without it. Note the direction: after the uncap a maximised desktop IS ultrawide, so the retired sentence argued for a number it would no longer have chosen. 🔴 AND THE HEADROOM STATED IN THIS ENTRY WAS ALSO WRONG, IN BLOCK-WIDTH TERMS. Every version of the argument above compares 1800 against the BLOCK's width; the threshold is not applied to that number. useUltrawide observes the element carrying shellStyle, which has padding: SHELL_PADDING (24px a side), and its steady-state reading is ResizeObserver's contentRect.width — the CONTENT box. So the real crossing point is 1848px of block width, not 1800, and the margin at a maximised 1920px browser is 57px (1905 - 48 - 1800) rather than the 105px this entry implied. The seed taken right after observe() reads el.clientWidth, the PADDING box, so it crosses at 1800: a block 1800-1847px wide paints one frame at four columns and settles at three. That content-box/padding-box split is the SDK's own — dist/hooks/useBlockBreakpoint.js reads `entries[0]?.contentRect.width ?? el.clientWidth` and seeds from el.clientWidth, verified in the installed package — and useUltrawide mirrors it deliberately so the tier and the ultrawide flag are never measured against two different boxes. The BEHAVIOUR is therefore left alone; what was corrected is the reasoning at layout.ts's ULTRAWIDE_MIN docblock, which argued in block-width terms and never mentioned the 48px.

decisions.fork: Trust the ultrawide flag, or clamp it to the tier?
decisions.chosen: Clamp, but by LADDER POSITION rather than by the literal `tier === 'xl'`: the 4-column branch requires `ultrawide && admitsUltrawide(tier)`, which is true for xl and for any tier the SDK adds above it.
decisions.constraint: The two values come from two independent ResizeObservers and can disagree during a resize frame; a caller or a test can also pass a combination no real geometry produces (`('sm', true)`, `('lg', true)`). Taking the tier as the authority makes the 4-column branch unreachable except from a block that is genuinely wide enough for both — >=1440 by the tier, and clearing ULTRAWIDE_MIN on the box useUltrawide measures (the CONTENT box in steady state, i.e. >=1848px of block width; see the ultrawide fork's headroom correction). 🔴 THE SPELLING WAS `tier === 'xl'` AND THAT SILENTLY HARDCODED SOMETHING THIS APP DOES NOT OWN. BREAKPOINT_KEYS belongs to @civitai/theme; nothing pinned xl as its last element. Add a 2xl and resolveBlockTier(2560) returns '2xl', which reaches the rail branch as it should but was clamped OUT of wide — the widest screens quietly losing the fourth column and the 400px rail, with every test green because they only ever pinned 1440 -> 'xl'. 🔴 THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT THE FIX WAS WRONG IN THE OTHER DIRECTION, AND THE EXISTING SUITE CAUGHT IT: clamping to 'any tier that gets the rail' admitted ('lg', true), which would hand a 1184px block four columns and a 400px rail — lg spans 1184-1439, so no block >=1800px can ever report it. Recorded because the near-miss is the useful part. 🔴 A SECOND ATTEMPT WAS ALSO ABANDONED: computing the admissible set at module load by probing resolveBlockTier. Correct, but it made a pure layout module call the SDK at import time and broke three existing suites that partially mock @civitai/blocks-react without that export — a real cost for a cosmetic gain. What ships instead is an app-owned ladder mirrored in layout.ts, with an unrecognised tier treated as wider than xl. That assumption is STATED, not hidden: it is right for a tier appended above xl (the defect, and the only direction the scale has grown) and would be wrong for one inserted below, so layout.test.ts pins the ladder's contents AND its gaplessness against resolveBlockTier — a first-party export — so an insertion anywhere fails loudly and a human decides. BREAKPOINT_KEYS is deliberately NOT imported, in shipped code or in tests: @civitai/theme is a transitive dependency here, pinned by @civitai/blocks-react and absent from this app's package.json, and no @civitai/* version was added or hand-edited by this round.

decisions.fork: brandDepth: accent (host tokens) or skin (app palette)?
decisions.constraint: Explicitly requested for this pass. It transfers light/dark correctness to the app, so the rubric's dual-theme check became mandatory: every surface/border/text pair is asserted in BOTH themes, and the contrast is COMPUTED rather than eyeballed.

decisions.fork: Implement the palette as cascading CSS custom properties or a typed TS object?
decisions.chosen: A typed TS object keyed by theme (`palette.dark.surface`), consumed through the existing inline-style objects.
decisions.constraint: jsdom does not resolve the cascade for custom properties — getComputedStyle hands back the literal `var(--x)` text — so a var()-based palette could only be asserted as 'a string that mentions a token name'. Under skin the dual-theme assertion is mandatory; a structural check that type-checks past a wrong value would make that assertion dishonest.

decisions.fork: Does `skin` mean restyling the W6 pack's components too?
decisions.chosen: No. The app palette owns the surfaces the APP draws (shell, hero, rail, field chrome, pill rows, format cards, board, candidate grid). Button/Alert/Card/Textarea/TextInput/Slider/SegmentedControl/Badge keep theming themselves from the pack stylesheet.
decisions.constraint: The pack styles itself from `data-theme` on the block root, which the app already sets; fighting it would mean overriding a stylesheet the app does not own, in both themes, with no way to assert the result in jsdom. Both families read the same `data-theme`, so they flip together.

decisions.fork: Secondary text: keep `color: token` + `opacity: 0.8`, or an explicit dim token?
decisions.chosen: An explicit `textDim` token, and `opacity` removed from the affected surfaces.
decisions.constraint: Under skin the contrast of every text pair IS the claim, and an opacity on top of a token makes the realized ratio a number no test can read off the palette. Measured: textDim is 7.84:1 on dark page, 6.62:1 on light. Same change for the hero sub-line, which under light theme had been pushed below AA by its opacity.

decisions.fork: The :focus-visible ring was still painted in the HOST's accent. Give it a new palette token, reuse `brand`, or duplicate the hex into CSS?
decisions.chosen: Reuse `brand`, and hand it to the stylesheet as one inherited custom property `--yt-focus-ring`, set inline on the block root by shellStyle from palette[theme].brand.
decisions.constraint: The ring was `var(--civitai-color-primary)` — correct while brandDepth was `accent` and the app borrowed the host's hue, and wrong the moment this pass declared `skin`: it was the one piece of chrome the skin did not reach, so a keyboard user got an outline in a colour appearing nowhere else on the block. Pre-existing, but squarely inside this pass's scope. Not a NEW token, because palette.ts's own rule is that a token only one surface uses is a surface that should have reused one. Not a hex in CSS either: that would be a second copy of the brand in a file with no access to the TS palette, needing a prefers-color-scheme branch that the host's data-theme would not agree with. An inherited property keeps the value in palette.ts, where it is already asserted in both themes, and custom properties inherit so one declaration on the block root covers every control the app draws. Graded at the bar that governs a focus indicator (WCAG 1.4.11, 3:1 non-text) against all five app-drawn grounds a ring can land on: worst case 4.20:1 (light, brand on brandTint) against 5.87:1 in dark. Two guards meet at the seam — palette.test.ts pins the complete set of `outline` declarations index.css ships, and responsive.test.tsx pins that the App sets the property from the right theme; either alone leaves the ring falling through to the currentColor fallback with nothing failing. NOT claimed: whether this outline also wins over the W6 pack's own focus styling on the PACK's components. jsdom performs no cascade, so that is unmeasured.

decisions.fork: What goes in the persistent rail at lg+, and what goes in the main column?
decisions.chosen: Rail (sticky, 340px / 400px ultrawide): mode toggle, prompt, model, LoRAs, images-per-format, spend-from, Generate, and the three PRE-spend gates. Main: hero above both, then results, then the format picker.
decisions.constraint: The ask names prompt/model/LoRA for the rail. The format picker went to main because it is the surface that wants width (usable previews), and results went above it because they are the app's primary object once they exist (phase 2). Post-spend reporting (the server's spend figure, per-format failures) moved to the results block so it sits beside what it describes; pre-spend gates stayed next to the button that triggers them.

decisions.fork: Below lg, where does the format picker sit relative to the Generate button?
decisions.chosen: Between the prompt and the model control, as before — which is why the inputs are two fragments rather than one `controls` constant.
decisions.constraint: The format count IS the workflow count, so the picker decides the bill. Putting it after Generate would ask people to choose formats after paying.

decisions.fork: The rail was asked for as 'persistent'. Make it position:sticky?
decisions.chosen: Yes — position: sticky, BOUNDED: top: SHELL_PADDING, maxHeight: calc(100dvh - 2*SHELL_PADDING), overflowY: auto, alignSelf: start. It is LIVE on both host surfaces, and the two-column arrangement is a second, independent form of persistence on top of it.
decisions.constraint: 🔴 THIS ENTRY CORRECTS A FINDING THE PASS FIRST GOT BACKWARDS, AND THE CORRECTION IS THE POINT. The version of it that shipped at 6fcd076 said sticky was 'almost certainly inert in production' because useBlockResize posts RESIZE_IFRAME so the host fits the iframe to content. That was reasoned from the hook's docs and never measured, and it is false on BOTH surfaces a block can be mounted in (read off civitai@main). FULL PAGE (/apps/run/<slug>, the only surface wide enough to reach the lg rail at all): PageBlockHost.tsx handles no RESIZE_IFRAME message at all — IframeHost.tsx is the only host component that does, verified by grep across src/components/AppBlocks/*.tsx — and it sizes the frame `height: 100%` with `min-height: calc(100dvh - <site header>)`, so the frame is viewport-height whatever the app reports and the app's content scrolls INSIDE it. SLOT (IframeHost.tsx): RESIZE_IFRAME is honoured, but the reported height goes through clampBlockHeight, which takes the minimum of the request, the manifest's maxHeight, a hard ceiling, and the viewport less the host's own chrome; past that clamp the frame stops growing and the app scrolls internally here too. So the rail genuinely stays on screen while the candidate grid scrolls past it — the feature is better than the first version of this entry claimed. useBlockResize is still called and still right (it is what lets a SHORT block occupy only the height it needs in a slot), but 'the host fits the iframe to content' is not a property that survives either surface. Still NOT confirmed in pixels: jsdom performs no layout, so what the tests can assert is the declaration, and the browser check is the existing capture deferred item. 🔴 AND THE VERSION THAT SHIPPED STICKY UNBOUNDED MADE THE SPEND BUTTON REACHABLE ONLY BY LUCK. `position: sticky; top: 0` with no maxHeight and no overflow is WORSE than no sticky at all once the rail is taller than the scrollport: the frame's scroll moves the MAIN column, the rail cannot scroll its own overflow, and its tail — quantity, spend-from, Generate, and the needs-consent / insufficient / account-rejected alerts that gate the spend — sits below the fold for the whole sticky range. On a 1280x800 laptop (>=1184 so the rail is on; the frame is min-height: calc(100dvh - header), about 740px of scrollport) with 5 LoRAs added, the rail exceeds the scrollport and the control that debits the viewer's Buzz is off-screen at every scroll position where the prompt is visible. Not strictly unreachable — at the travel limit the rail unsticks — but it inverts the rail's purpose. Bounded now, and BOTH numbers are derived from SHELL_PADDING rather than picked: top is one inset (top: 0 sat flush against the frame's top edge, ignoring the inset the shell gives every other edge) and the bound is 100dvh less two insets, the height the shell's box leaves inside the frame. maxHeight WITHOUT overflowY would be worse again — it would CLIP the Generate button instead of stranding it — so the pair ships together and responsive.test.tsx asserts both. NOT VERIFIED IN PIXELS: jsdom performs no layout, so nothing observes the rail travelling, overflowing or scrolling; what is asserted is that the bound and the overflow are present in the emitted style and that both are expressed in terms of SHELL_PADDING. The travel itself is in deferred[].

decisions.fork: The boot skeleton in index.html is a SECOND surface the skin never reached. Leave it, restyle it onto the palette, or delete the bootSkeleton opt-in?
decisions.chosen: Restyle it onto the palette (page / surface / surfaceRaised / border in both themes) and replace its single 640px cap with layoutForTier's three-rung ladder, guarded by src/boot-skeleton.test.ts which parses the shipped HTML.
decisions.constraint: block.manifest.json declares bootSkeleton: true, so the Civitai run host stands down its own loading veil and index.html IS the loading state. It still painted the W6 pack's old greys (#101113 / #1a1b1e / #2c2e33) inside a 640px cap, so at 1905px a viewer saw a 640px dark-grey card centred on near-black snap to a full-width #0B0E14 page with a 340px rail: a width jump AND a colour jump. 🔴 THE FIX CREATES A DUPLICATE, AND THAT IS THE REAL HAZARD. index.html is static — it cannot import palette.ts or call layoutForTier — so every value moved onto the palette is a second copy of a number TypeScript owns, and a silently drifting duplicate reads as deliberate. src/boot-skeleton.test.ts therefore parses the shipped <style> block and compares each declaration against its source, CLOSED in both directions: a colour no ledger row accounts for is itself a failure. Per-declaration rather than set-equality, because comparing the SET would pass while surface and surfaceRaised were SWAPPED — verified by mutation: the swap goes red on both ledger rows while the set check stays green. Two further mutants watched red: reverting one hex to its old grey, and re-instating the 640px cap at lg. 🔴 THE RUNGS ARE VIEWPORT MEDIA QUERIES AND THE APP IS NOT. App.tsx passes rootRef to useBlockBreakpoint, and that element carries padding: SHELL_PADDING, so the width the app grades is the viewport LESS SHELL_INSET (48px). The rungs are OFFSET by it — @media min-width 816px and 1232px against the app's own 768 and 1184 — which takes the card-vs-column disagreement from 48 viewport widths (worst 127px at 815px) to zero across 300–2600px. A CONTAINER query is still impossible for the reason layout.ts gives. NOT changed: the favicon's #1971c2, outside the <style> block and not a boot-skeleton surface.

decisions.fork: The dual-theme guard covered 8 surfaces by hand and left ~14 uncovered. Add the missing 14, or make the guard mechanical?
decisions.chosen: Mechanical, in two halves that grade different things: GUARD A forbids any colour literal in the two files that draw the app (a property of the whole file, so a surface added tomorrow is covered the moment it is written), and GUARD B walks the rendered DOM in both themes and grades every painted text colour against its own RESOLVED ground at AA. Both in src/theme-guard.test.tsx. The 8 hand-written surface assertions stay — they pin WHICH token each key surface uses, which neither mechanical guard can.
decisions.constraint: responsive.test.tsx stated this exact hazard in its own words and then covered eight surfaces, leaving previewPlaceholderStyle, checkStyle, FormatEditor's inputStyle/counterStyle/errorStyle, PublishedBoard's boardStyle/boardRowStyle/boardSuffixStyle/dimStyle, loraRowStyle, canvasStyle, sourceThumbStyle and colorInputStyle with no coverage at all. Demonstrated: mutating FormatPicker.tsx's cardButtonStyle from `color: pal.text` to the dark theme's own literal '#F7F9FC' left the whole suite green while rendering format-card labels at 1.055:1 on light `surface` and 1.105:1 on light `brandTint`. Adding 14 more hand-written assertions would regenerate the gap at the 15th surface. 🔴 AND THE OBVIOUS MECHANICAL FIX DOES NOT WORK — recorded because it is the trap. 'Assert every painted colour is a member of palette[theme]' passes on this mutant: '#F7F9FC' IS palette.light.page and palette.light.overlayFg. So does the cross-theme form 'the dark value and the light value must be the same TOKEN', because (PAPER, PAPER) is exactly the pair overlayFg has in both themes. The value is a legitimate palette colour; what is wrong is WHERE it is used, so the guard has to grade a RELATIONSHIP — foreground against its own ground — not membership. Guard B resolves that ground by walking ancestors, compositing translucent layers and returning every stop of a gradient, and it asserts a non-zero walk (24 element/ground pairs per theme, measured) BEFORE its verdict so a guard that observed nothing fails loudly instead of passing vacuously. Both guards were watched RED on the exact mutant: Guard A names the offending surface (#F7F9FC in cardButtonStyle), Guard B reports 6 of 24 pairs below AA in the light theme and correctly stays green in dark, where the value is right.

decisions.fork: Which copy to delete under phase 2?
decisions.chosen: Deleted: the prompt description's restatement of the 1280x720 crop (the hero says it and the download button repeats it); the LoRA row's 'Optional. Up to 5, each with a weight.' (the 0/5 badge, the slider and the cap message already say all of it); 'pick one to edit' from the candidate count (every card carries an 'Edit & download' button). KEPT: every cost disclosure, the anonymous-persistence note, and the 'a preference, the server picks the final pool' honesty line.
decisions.constraint: The rubric forbids a paragraph that explains what the adjacent control already shows, and separately requires that any cost or partial-truth disclosure stays. The three deletions are the first kind; the three keeps are the second. 🔴 TWO CORRECTIONS TO THIS ENTRY. (1) The deleted LoRA string was mis-quoted here as 'Up to 3' and the badge as '0/3'. MAX_LORAS is 5 (src/models.ts:49, unchanged at both the base commit and this branch's head), so the real copy said 'Up to 5' and the badge reads '0/5'. The deletion itself was right; only this record of it was wrong, and a wrong quote of deleted copy is unreviewable — nobody can check a deletion against a string that never existed. (2) 'KEPT: every cost disclosure' was recorded as a decision WITH NO TEST BEHIND IT, in the same pass that deleted three adjacent strings. decisions.fork: How to assert a layout in an environment that performs no layout?
decisions.chosen: Two halves that meet at a named seam: layout.test.ts pins the NUMBERS layoutForTier returns with hand-written literals; responsive.test.tsx renders the real App at every tier and asserts those numbers reached the DOM — as the inline gridTemplateColumns/maxWidth a browser would read wherever a style carries the fact, and as a data-* attribute only where no style does.
decisions.constraint: jsdom computes no geometry, so neither half alone is evidence: the pure function could be right while the component ignored it, and the component could thread a value the function computes wrongly. 🔴 THE FIRST VERSION OF THIS SHIPPED BOTH WITNESSES FOR THE SAME FACTS, WHICH IS ONE WITNESS TOO MANY. data-max-width, data-rail and the results grid's data-columns each sat beside an inline-style assertion of the same number, so the production DOM carried three attributes whose only consumer was a duplicate assertion — and a second place to fall out of step. They are deleted. The inline style is the stronger of the two: a browser acts on it, so it cannot be right while the layout is wrong. What remains is the residue with no style twin: data-result-columns (decided at every tier, but only reaches a grid template once candidates exist), data-min-card, data-ultrawide (the app-owned threshold has no CSS form at all) and data-block-tier / data-layout / data-theme, which pre-date this pass.
